Session 3 :: Data Visualization with ggplot2

Learning objectives

By the end of this session you should be able to:

  • Say why ggplot2 is worth learning on top of base R graphics.
  • Read a ggplot2 call as three parts: data, aesthetic mapping, and geoms.
  • Reproduce the everyday plots you already make in base R — scatter, bar, histogram, boxplot — in ggplot2, and see the two side by side.
  • Add a grouping variable, split into panels, and fit a line per group with a small change to the code.
  • Save a figure at a resolution suitable for a manuscript.

This session is built around comparison. Almost every plotting slide shows base R on the left and ggplot2 on the right, so people can map what they already know onto the new syntax.

Why ggplot2?

The motivation

The same scatter plot, two ways

Base R

plot(Sepal.Width ~ Sepal.Length, data = iris)

ggplot2

ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point()

For a single, simple plot the two are close. The difference shows up as soon as the plot needs to grow.

Set expectations honestly: for a one-off scatter, base R is not worse. The argument for ggplot2 is about what happens next, not this slide.

Quick check — fixed colour vs mapped colour

Before we go further, compare these two base R calls:

cols <- c("#E69F00", "#0072B2", "#009E73")

# A
plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width, col = "blue")
# B
plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width, col = cols[iris$Species])
  • Your answer first
  • Answer

One of these sets a fixed colour; the other looks up a colour per observation from Species. Which is which, and what would you need to add to B to also get a legend?

A is fixed — every point is the same blue, no matter what. B is mapped — the colour depends on the data, so it varies row by row, and B is also the one that needs you to build a legend by hand in base R. ggplot2 makes exactly this distinction explicit: mappings go inside aes(), fixed values go outside it. We will put this to work right away.

This is the single idea the rest of the session hangs on. If people are solid on fixed-vs-mapped here, the “colour and legend” and “quiz Q1” slides later are mostly reinforcement.

Legends, panels, and styling

Three common tasks when a plot grows:

  1. Legends: base R uses legend(); ggplot2 generates guides from mappings.
  2. Panels: base R uses layouts and separate plotting calls; ggplot2 uses facets.
  3. Styling: base R shares settings through par() or helpers; ggplot2 uses themes.

We will compare these workflows using the same data.

Both systems support reusable styling. Focus on how ggplot2 coordinates mappings, guides, and panels as a plot develops. Source: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/graphics/html/par.html

The idea: a grammar of graphics

A ggplot2 plot is built from a few named pieces:

Piece Question it answers Example
data Which data frame? iris
aesthetic mapping (aes) Which column drives which visual property? x = Sepal.Length, colour = Species
geom How should the data be displayed? geom_point(), geom_bar()
facet Split into panels by which variable? facet_wrap(~ Species)
scale How do data values map to a visual range — position, colour, size? scale_colour_*(), scale_x_log10()
theme How does the plot look — fonts, gridlines, background — independent of the data? theme_minimal(), theme_classic()

Some geoms display individual observations; others display summaries. Layers inherit data and mappings from ggplot() unless overridden.

Use + to add geoms, facets, scales, labels, or themes to the initial plot. A point usually represents one observation, while a bar or boxplot can summarize many observations. Keep these examples brief.

Anatomy of a ggplot() call

ggplot(data = iris,                                  # 1. the data
       mapping = aes(x = Sepal.Length,               # 2. map columns
                     y = Sepal.Width,                #    to visual
                     colour = Species)) +            #    properties
  geom_point() +                                     # 3. draw points
  labs(x = "Sepal length (cm)",                      # 4. labels
       y = "Sepal width (cm)")
  • data and mapping set once in ggplot() are inherited by every layer, unless a layer overrides them.
  • Use + to add layers or settings. Later drawing layers appear on top.
  • aes() is for mappings from data. A fixed value (all points blue) goes outside aes().

The aes-vs-fixed distinction is the single most common beginner confusion. Flag it here and it comes back in the quiz.

Feature by feature

base R on the left, ggplot2 on the right

Colour and legend from a variable

Base R — formula interface, own legend

cyl_f <- factor(mtcars$cyl)
cols  <- c("#E69F00", "#0072B2", "#009E73")
plot(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars,
     col = cols[cyl_f], pch = 16)
legend("topright", legend = levels(cyl_f),
       col = cols, pch = 16,
       title = "cyl", bty = "n")

ggplot2 — one mapping, legend appears

ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg,
                   colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(colour = "cyl")

Both plots use column names for axis labels. In ggplot2, mapping colour = factor(cyl) assigns colours and creates the legend.

Numeric cyl would give a continuous colour scale. factor(cyl) treats the cylinder counts as categories. The palettes differ between these examples; the comparison concerns the grouping and legend workflow.

Bar chart of counts

Base R — tabulate first, then plot

tab <- table(mtcars$cyl)
barplot(tab,
        xlab = "Cylinders",
        ylab = "Count")

ggplot2 — counting is built in

ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "Count")

geom_bar() counts the rows in each category for you. If you already have the numbers, use geom_col() instead.

Histogram

Define the bin boundaries once for both plots:

brks <- seq(10, 35, by = 2.5)

Base R

hist(mtcars$mpg, breaks = brks,
     xlab = "MPG", main = "")

ggplot2

ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = brks)

Both plots use the same explicit breakpoints, so the bins are comparable.

Define brks once before running either example. A numeric breaks = 10 in hist() is a suggestion: base R selects pretty boundaries. ggplot2’s bins uses a different binning procedure; matching the number alone does not ensure matching boundaries. Both examples use right-closed bins. Sources: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/graphics/html/hist.html https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_histogram.html

Boxplot by group

Base R — formula interface

boxplot(mpg ~ cyl, data = mtcars,
        xlab = "Cylinders", ylab = "MPG")

ggplot2 — x and y as a mapping

ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl), mpg)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Cylinders", y = "MPG")

The base R formula mpg ~ cyl becomes the mapping aes(factor(cyl), mpg).

A minor technical difference, usually only worth mentioning if asked: boxplot()’s hinges come from boxplot.stats()/fivenum(), while geom_boxplot() uses the 25th/75th percentile with quantile type 7. Their hinges can differ, especially for small samples. Source: https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_boxplot.html

Small multiples: base R code

Set up the panels, use shared limits, and plot each species.

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
xr <- range(iris$Sepal.Length)
yr <- range(iris$Sepal.Width)
for (sp in levels(iris$Species)) {
  plot(Sepal.Width ~ Sepal.Length, data = iris,
       subset = Species == sp,
       xlim = xr, ylim = yr, main = sp, pch = 16)
}
par(op)

The loop and shared limits are normal base R practice. par(op) restores the settings explicitly changed at the start. The formula supplies axis labels. The margin settings help three narrow panels fit on one device.

Small multiples: ggplot2 code

ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ Species)

facet_wrap() handles the panel layout, labels, and shared scales.

Fixed scales are the default. Changing the faceting variable updates the panels automatically. Source: https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/facet_wrap.html

Small multiples: compare the output

Base R

ggplot2

Both show one panel per species with common limits across panels.

A fitted line per group

Base R — fit and draw each line

cols  <- c("#E69F00", "#0072B2", "#009E73")
sp    <- iris$Species
plot(Sepal.Width ~ Sepal.Length, data = iris,
     col = cols[sp], pch = 16)
for (i in levels(sp)) {
  d <- iris[sp == i, ]
  abline(lm(Sepal.Width ~ Sepal.Length, d),
         col = cols[which(levels(sp) == i)])
}

ggplot2 — add a smooth layer

ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width,
                 colour = Species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

geom_smooth(method = "lm") fits one line per colour group, because the colour = Species mapping already split the data — the same fit the base R loop builds by hand.

Two details worth knowing but not dwelling on: abline() draws across the full plotting region, while geom_smooth() by default (fullrange = FALSE) only draws each line across that group’s own observed x-range, so the lines can look slightly different in length between the two panels. Adding facets in ggplot2 fits each model within its group and panel. To reproduce this in base R, explicitly subset for each panel and group. Source: https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_smooth.html

Styling and themes

Base R — share settings with par()

op <- par(cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1, las = 1)
plot(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars,
     pch = 16, col = "#0072B2")
par(op)

ggplot2 — a named, reusable theme

ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)

Both systems support reusable styling. ggplot2 packages plot styling in named theme objects, such as theme_classic().

The point colour is fixed outside aes(); it is a layer setting.

par() settings apply to subsequent base graphics plots on the current graphics device until changed or restored. They do not apply to every plot in the session or automatically carry over to a new PNG or PDF device. Base R helper functions can also bundle styling. In ggplot2, theme_set() sets a default theme for subsequent plots. Themes control non-data display components such as axis text, gridlines, and backgrounds. Sources: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/graphics/html/par.html https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/theme.html

A plot you can keep, not just draw

plot() writes straight to the graphics device — nothing is left afterward to reuse. A ggplot2 call instead returns an object.

p  <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + geom_point()
p2 <- p + facet_wrap(~ cyl)   # p2 is p, extended
p                              # p itself is unchanged
  • + returns a new object rather than changing p in place — p2 gains the facets, p does not.
  • Storing a plot in a variable lets you reuse it: display it, save several versions, or pass it into a function — build once, use for several purposes.
  • A bare p auto-prints at the console or top level of a chunk. Inside a function or loop, that does not happen automatically — call print(p) explicitly.

This sets up the next slide: p is not only a save-target, it is a general-purpose object. Contrast with base R, where plot() has no return value worth keeping — the drawing is a side effect, not a result. Source: https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/print.ggplot.html

Save a plot object

Base R — open a device, plot, close it

png("figure.png", width = 8, height = 5,
    units = "in", res = 300)
plot(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
dev.off()

ggplot2 — save the plot object p

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point()

ggsave("figure.png", p,
       width = 8, height = 5,
       units = "in", dpi = 300)

Choose dimensions, file format, and raster resolution to match the publication’s requirements. ggsave() infers the format from the extension.

Here, 8 by 5 inches at 300 dpi produces a 2400 by 1500 pixel PNG. For vector elements in a PDF, dpi does not determine sharpness. PDF files can also contain raster images, whose resolution still matters. Source: https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggsave.html

When base R is still a good choice

ggplot2 is not a replacement for every situation:

  • A quick look at a vector while you work — plot() or hist() is fast and needs no packages.
  • Base R objects with dedicated plot methods, e.g. plot(hclust_result) for a dendrogram or image() for a matrix.
  • Very custom, one-off diagrams where you want to place each element by hand.

The clearest advantages shown here are automatic legends, faceting, and reusing mappings across layers. Both systems can produce publication figures.

Ask which of these situations learners encounter in their own work.

Summary

Three things to take away

  1. A ggplot2 plot is data + an aesthetic mapping + geoms, combined with +.
  2. Mappings coordinate colours, groups, and legends; facets split the data into panels.
  3. aes() is for values that come from the data; fixed values go outside aes().

Extend the same structure with new geoms, scales, and themes.
